newsitem.title: USA: Corporate earnings may be reality check for stock market.
newsitem.headline: Corporate earnings may be reality check for stock market.

text.p: Time for a reality check for the greatest bull market in history?
The corporate earnings season heats up next week and Wall Street will get a clue as to whether stock prices are overblown after racking up their biggest quarterly gain in 10 years.
But for now, experts are advising investors to keep cool and not panic in the face of nervous times in this fast-rising market.
The betting is that if second-quarter earnings prove to be as good as many analysts expect, then the bull market will be intact, perhaps through year-end.

Stocks have been barrelling higher and in the last three months the Dow Jones industrial average has gained an eye-poppingly 1,225 points -- or 19 percent, making it the largest advance since March 1987, when it soared nearly 22 percent.

After a holiday-shortened trading week, the Dow closed Thursday with a gain of 100.43 points at a new high of 7,895.81, eclipsing its June 20 record finish of 7,796.51. For the week it was up 208.09 points.
The market's ascent has been fuelled by a near-perfect scenario of steady earnings growth and an economy that shows no signs of generating nasty inflation.
Another addition to the cheery scenario is Washington's deal to balance the federal budget, which could eventually bring lower interest rates.
To many experts, the market fundamentals appear to be a 'Can't lose, nothing-can-go wrong' situation. The rules of the game have not been changed, they say, and the goal posts have not been moved.
The bulls say the earnings story is still upbeat. On the interest rate front, things have improved now that the Fed is less of a threat to the market than it was early in the year.

The central bank, which has been standing by, waiting to pounce with another interest rate rise at the slightest hint of upward price pressure, will stay out of the picture as long as the economy slows and inflation is unable to build up a head of steam.

The Fed jacked up short-term rates in March for the first time in more than two years in an effort to brake the economy's speedy growth and keep inflation from rising. The move unleashed a selloff in stocks between March and April that wiped out almost 10 percent or 700 points from the blue-chip Dow index.
But the central bank has since kept its hands off interest rates in May and, most recently, this week, on signs that the economy was slowing on its own.
Data released this past week provided more proof that the econony is backpedalling after growing at a torrid pace early in the year.
The government reported that the unemployment rate rose to 5 percent in June from a 24-year low 4.8 percent in May.
In another report, the National Association of Purchasing Management's index -- a closely watched measure of industrial activity -- fell in June along with new orders and prices.
Also, construction spending in May sank 1.8 percent after rising by 0.3 percent in April. It was the biggest drop in more than three years, since a 3 percent slump in January 1994.
Despite the positive atmosphere, stocks are still vulnerable to the quarterly earnings test, and investors will get their first taste of corporate results in the coming week.

Many Wall Streeters believe that the market, which is one of the most the reliable economic indicators, will stand up to the earnings challenge. After the earnings odyssey, they see smooth sailing for the market.
A sampling of analysts' estimates shows that second-quarter profits will be positive and most of the bad news or so-called earnings surprises have already been pre-announced.

First Call, a Boston-based firm that tracks analysts' earnings forecasts, said the Standard and Poor's 500 companies are expected to report a 9.1-percent rise in second-quarter operating profits, vs. a gain in the first quarter of 15.1 percent.
But the company noted that analysts typically low-ball the earnings numbers by an average of 2.6 percent and the total will have to be adjusted higher.

"If we follow the normal pattern of the last three years, and given the normal negative pre-announcements, we should expect to get the usual positive bias," said Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call.
"When all the reporting is done, we should get something approaching 12 percent earnings gain over last year," he said.
Over the years, the earnings reporting season has been a nail-biting time for investors, who worry if their stocks would meet expectations.
But the trend among companies to pre-announce or provide earnings guidances has helped to blunt the impact of bad news.

"The motivation in confesssing their earnings early, particularly if it's negative, is that the companies expect they'll be penalised somewhat less than if they wait until the actual report is put out," Hill said.
He said the second quarter is proving to be "business as usual" as far as earnings pre-announcements.

First Call said it collected nearly 140 earnings warnings this past week and of that total, 61 percent were negative, while 39 percent were positive surprises. In last year's second quarter, 63 percent of the reporting companies had negative heads-up announcements.

Al Kugel, senior investment strategist for Stein Roe & Farnham, a Chicago-based mutual fund, said the market will stay on an upward course in the second half of the year, although the gain may not be as "sensational" as in the last three months.

"We are going into the second quarter with a strong market that is already anticipating good results, and it may be hard to get the same upward lift again," he said. "The market will do quite well but it won't be zooming out of the starting gate."
Kugel said that mutual fund investors are buying stocks for their long-term earnings prospects, and the positive outlook for the economy and inflation should keep the market sizzling.
"I don't see anything -- politically, economically, socially and internationally -- that could upset the positive environment," he said.
But others warned that the fastest market gains are often the quickest to be evaporate.
Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co., and a long-time Wall Street bear, views the earnings story differently and says now is not the time for heroes.

"Earnings will not get better in the second half of the year and I think we've passed the peak earnings period after corporations have been able to expand their profit margins, particularly in the second quarter," he said.
Metz said the earnings momentum will "slow down significantly" and the increase will shrink to a single-digit figure.

"Expectations that we will continue dramatic earnings momentum will be disappointing because the environment as far as earnings momentum, interest rates and inflation will become less-auspicious as the year progresses," he said.

Metz believes that the industrialised countries are headed into the most "vigorous" boom in a decade and the resulting rise in interest rates and inflation in the United States, Europe and Japan will put a lid on the stock market.
On Thursday, the Nasdaq composite index closed up 12.00 points at a new high of 1,467.61, up 29.46 points for the week.
The Standard & Poor's index of 500 stocks rose 12.89 to a new high of 916.92, for a gain of 29.62 on the week. The American Stock Exchange index was up 4.28 at 634.34, a gain of 14.27 for the week.
The NYSE composite index of all listed common stocks rose 5.97 to 477.68, a new high, and was up 14.38 for the week.
